title: five, and they read like kindness
hookLine: five, and they read like kindness

cards: When people hear a religion has rules, they brace. They picture a long list of thou-shalt-nots, somebody stern at the top, and a lot of guilt. Buddhism has a short list too.

Five lines. Buddhists say them at temples and at home, often every week, some every day, in a temple in Sri Lanka or a living room in Los Angeles. But read them closely and they don't sound like a list of rules.
They sound like a promise to be easy to live next to.

teach.b: The precepts. In Pali, sila: conduct, virtue, the way you live.
There are five for lay Buddhists. Not to kill or harm living beings. Not to take what isn't given.
Not to cause harm through sex. Not to speak falsely. And not to take intoxicants that cloud the mind.
That's the list. Now listen to how they're actually said.
Each one is phrased the same way: I undertake the training rule to refrain from harming living beings. I undertake the training rule to refrain from taking what is not given. And so on.
Notice the words. I undertake. Nobody is ordering anyone.
You take them on yourself. And training rule. Not a law, not a commandment.
Something you practice, fail at sometimes, and pick up again, the way you'd train for a race. There's a teaching in the discourses that turns the whole thing around.
It calls the five precepts five great gifts. When you keep them, the Buddha says, you give freedom from fear to countless beings. Everyone near you can relax.
They don't have to worry you'll hurt them, rob them, betray them, lie to them, or lose control. And because you give them safety, you get to share in that safety too.
That's why they read like kindness. They aren't about keeping yourself pure. They're about everyone else being able to breathe around you.
Buddhists hold them in different ways. Some take all five for life. Some take them fresh on holy days.
Monks and nuns take many more.

how: Lay Buddhists often recite the five precepts in Pali after taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, at temple services, festivals and at home; some keep eight precepts on observance days.

games.q: what's inside the precepts — tap the pairs.
p: nobody orders it; you take it on

s: the precepts are commandments given by a god
each is a training rule that a person undertakes for themselves.
one discourse calls the five precepts great gifts
keeping them gives freedom from fear to countless beings.
monks and nuns keep only these five
they take many more. the five are for lay Buddhists.

games.q: you've taken the precept not to speak falsely. yesterday you told a lie. what does 'training rule' suggest you do?
o: give up the precept. you've failed.
pick it up again and keep training.
games.why: a training rule is practiced like a skill. you slip, notice, and take it up again. that's why many Buddhists recite the precepts regularly.

practice: The bell gives you about forty-five seconds. Think about the five: not harming, not taking, not betraying, not lying, not clouding the mind. Don't grade yourself.
Just ask which one would make the biggest difference to the people around you this week. Picture someone near you feeling a little safer because of it, and rest there.

wordCard.voice: The precepts. Five training rules, taken on freely, that give everyone around you freedom from fear. Twelfth word.

orig.note: Pali: the five precepts. pañca, five; sīla, conduct, virtue.

carryVoice: Your line: do less harm. It's a training rule, not a test you pass or fail. That's day twelve.
